Q: What is the real difference between a junior and senior developer? A:

As to the university, the best approach is paying maximum attention for the fundamentals rather than particular products and trendy topics.

It's important to beware of the illusion of knowledge. Your knowledge is only real if everything you learn is maintained by regular and thorough practice, even perfectionism.

One of the important points: the sooner you start developing real projects, the better. It may look difficult and even not realistic, but in real life there are many simple problems that could solve for yourself, your friends, family members, and other people. Think of something that could help to organize your everyday chores, hobby, and the like.

Q: Javascript: the code after `yield` is never executed A:

How are you verifying that the code after the yield never executes?

If it really doesn't execute then I suspect either your authenticate method is triggering a transition or your API promise is rejecting. Log the resolved promise to see what you are getting back. Put some logging into your catch and finally sections to see what is actually happening. Replace your API call with something like timeout(1000) to simplify the testing.

Is your trackEvent a promise or synchronous code?

In recent versions of Ember/Ember-concurrency you can use the async/await pattern which you might find easier than the yield and generator task* pattern

Q: Opendaylight Restconf always answers 401 A:

Have you tried following the OpenDaylight NETCONF user guide?

It seems like you're attempting to use the /restconf/ endpoint (draft-bierman-netconf-restconf-02) instead of /rests/ URI (RFC8040).

The draft-bierman-netconf-restconf-02 implementation is no longer available in recent OpenDaylight releases.

For more details, you can refer to the following links:

draft-bierman vs. RFC8040 ONAP RESTCONF Migration

Q: Create file using Shell Scripting A:

If by created in the desired directory you mean that the target directory should be created on demand, your best bet is New-Item, with the -Force switch.

# *Creates* (or replaces) the specified file as an empty file,
# creating its directory on demand.
# Outputs a [System.IO.FileInfo] instance representing the new file.
New-Item -Force c:\path\that\may\not\exist\yet\NewFile.txt

While you can use New-Item alone to also provide the new file's content, it has to be provided as a single input string; that is, 'foo', 'bar' | New-Item -Force c:\path\to\NewFile.txt does not work as intended; use 'foo', 'bar' | Out-String | New-Item -Force c:\path\to\NewFile.txt instead, though the alternatives discussed below may be preferable, not least because this approach requires buffering all output in memory first.
Note that BOM-less UTF-8 character encoding is invariably used, even in Windows PowerShell (which otherwise does not support creating files with this encoding using its file-saving cmdlets; by contrast, PowerShell (Core) 7 consistently defaults to BOM-less UTF-8).

However, given that New-Item outputs a [System.IO.FileInfo] representing the new file and given that this instances stringifies to the file's full (absolute) path, you can combine it with file-saving cmdlets such as Out-File and Set-Content, as well as with >, the redirection operator, which is in effect an alias of Out-File; this offers two advantages: (except with >) you can control the character encoding via the -Encoding parameter and you can use pipeline output to stream the content object by object to the file in a memory-efficient manner:

# Combine > with New-Item to *both create and stream output to* the target file.
# Alternatively, use, e.g., the following which allows you to add an -Encoding argument.
#   'foo', 'bar' | Out-File -LiteralPath (New-Item -Force c:\path\to\NewFile.txt)
'foo', 'bar' > (New-Item -Force c:\path\to\NewFile.txt)

Note:

  • Since > uses Out-File behind the scenes, the latter's default character encoding is used, which is "Unicode" (UTF-16LE) in Windows PowerShell vs. BOM-less UTF-8 in PowerShell (Core) 7

  • The only exception is in PowerShell (Core) 7 with output from external executables (as opposed to PowerShell-native commands), whose raw byte output is saved (but note that this does not apply to explicit use of Out-File).

  • For more information regarding character encoding / raw byte capture considerations, see this answer. Notably, when raw byte capture is not involved, the external-program output is only properly decoded if [Console]::OutputEncoding matches the actual output character encoding, before it is re-encoded based on the file-saving cmdlet's default / specified encoding.

  • As for when to choose > / Out-File vs. Set-Content:

    • The choice only matters with respect to output from PowerShell-native commands.

    • With non-string output, > / Out-File stringifies objects using PowerShell's rich for-display representations, as you would see when outputting to the console; by contrast, Set-Content uses simple .ToString() stringification, which with types other than strings and .NET primitive types is often unhelpful; conversely, if Set-Content's stringifications are sufficient (e.g. with output that already are strings), Set-Content performs better; see this answer for more information.

Q: How to fit a circle onto a weathered pipe? A:

You should probably use a method of determining the severity of erosion that doesn't rely on this. How do you intend to calculate the erosion? It's likely that the same value, or a similar value, can be calculated without fitting a circle.
